1:
Who the kine of Bashan are is the chapter's first dispute, and it turns on the feminine forms. Ellicott takes them for the luxurious women of fashion in Samaria, addressing their husbands as masters and calling for drink paid for out of the robbery of the poor; he reports the alternative that the feminines are sarcastic epithets for effeminate men and calls it not a probable explanation. Keil and Delitzsch agree, heading the passage as the shameful captivity coming on the voluptuous and wanton women of the city. Gill reports the rabbinic identification with the wives of kings and princes, and supposes a herdsman might in his rustic manner so compliment the court ladies for their plumpness and petulancy, but himself thinks the great men are meant, named for their effeminacy and perhaps with a glance at the calves they worshipped. Wesley and Henry both take the rulers, and Clarke will have it either way, the iniquitous and idle drones whether men or women.

The figure itself is explained from the country and from the prophet's trade. Ellicott places Bashan in the rich pasture east of the river, where cattle flourished, and recalls the strong bulls of that region used elsewhere of an ideal sufferer's enemies. Clarke says such an address was quite natural from a herdsman of Tekoa, and makes the point of it that fatted bullocks are shortly led out to slaughter. Henry works the herdsman's dialect hardest: the cattle of that breed were large and strong and grew wanton on fat pasture, would not be kept within their own bounds but broke the hedges and fences to trespass on the neighbours' ground, and gored the smaller cattle that were no match for them. Wesley puts the same in a line, full-fed and wanton beasts that push at and hurt the weaker of the herd.

Calvin begins by quarrelling with the chapter division. Whoever made it, he says, cannot have considered the argument, since the prophet is still reproving the rich men he had been threatening before. He then supplies the scorn he hears in the epithet. The great and pompous will despise the threatening, think themselves not exposed to judgment, take the reproof as a wrong, and ask how a shepherd dares assail them so boldly; to which the prophet answers that he makes no account of the greatness they pride themselves on, their wealth amounting to no more than fatness.

The oath is read for what it puts at stake. Gill takes swearing by his holiness as swearing by himself, holiness being his nature and an essential attribute, the oath given so that men may be assured the thing will be performed; he reports the rendering by his holy place, understood of heaven, and thinks it unlikely. Wesley says the same more briefly, by himself as he is the holy God, and identifies the days threatened as those of famine, desolation and captivity.

The hooks produce the widest divergence in the tile. Clarke distinguishes two kinds of fishing, the rod and baited hook for small fish and the gaff for large ones taken in the rivers or the sea, and matches them to common people and to the powerful; he then returns to the gender question and says the prophet speaks by a figure, meaning men of effeminate manners and idle lives, not the bulls of Bashan but the cows. Ellicott keeps the image simple, describing the suddenness and irresistible character of the seizure by which men in fancied security are carried off; but he records how strange the imagery has seemed, and cites a translator who renders instead that they shall be driven into thorny districts and among thorn bushes. Wesley names the instrument, the Assyrian army, and extends the sentence to the children of the oppressors.
3:
The going out at the breaches is the end of the fishing figure for some and plain siege for others. Clarke keeps the metaphor running: the women are caught by hooks or nets, and though they tear the net by their flouncing they are taken out at those very tears; the city is the net, and what looks like escape is capture. Gill takes it literally and finds a symmetry: those who had broken the fences of law and justice now find their own city walls broken and are glad to escape through them with their lives. Ellicott renders the first clause each one straight before her, women going tamely out through the breaches into captivity.

Ellicott admits the next clause defeats him. He takes the verb as passive, ye shall be thrown out, and turns to the noun the English renders the palace, which assumes the word here is another form of one used elsewhere in the book; that, he says, is guess-work and yields no good sense. He prefers a slight emendation making the obscure word a proper name, which the old versions support. Calvin declines the philology and keeps to the tone: the prophet still addresses the judges and the king's counsellors and still refuses to count these pompous masters as men, which is the more pointed because the rich observe their ranks so strictly and are so hard to approach. Keil and Delitzsch head the passage in one line: Israel would not leave its idolatry, so the Lord would go on visiting the people with judgments.

The summons to the shrines is read as irony by all, and they compete to sharpen it. Gill says the words give no liberty to sin but reprove it, bidding them go on and mark the issue. Wesley calls it a strong irony that gives them over as incorrigible. Clarke turns the knife on the place, since the site named second was where the reproach of their fathers had been rolled away and should have stayed sacred; let them keep offering morning and evening to senseless gods and supporting a vicious priesthood with tithes that should have gone to God's service. Ellicott notes that the sarcastic force disappears in the English.

Two details in the ironical liturgy are argued over. Ellicott would read every three days rather than every three years, since the law required a tithe only every third year, and takes the prophet to be lashing them with hyperbole for their excessive generosity to base priests and spurious sanctuaries. Wesley keeps the three years and cites the law that appointed them. On the leaven Ellicott corrects the rendering to offer by burning your thank-offering of leaven, and observes that leaven was never allowed in a sacrifice made by fire, so the prophet ironically calls on them to break a law he knew they habitually broke. Wesley agrees it is against the express law and adds the dare, do so at your peril and see whether it ends well. Gill dissents: leaven was forbidden in one kind of offering but ordered with the thanksgiving, and he follows a rabbi in taking the clause as lawful in itself and ironically commanded only because it is offered to idols.

Calvin draws the doctrine the irony serves. The people thought their worship fully approved because they sacrificed at those shrines; the prophet shows that the harder they laboured at sacred things the more grievously they offended and the heavier the judgment they earned. What do you gain, he has the prophet ask, by wearying yourselves to omit nothing the law prescribes, except to provoke God's wrath more and more? Clarke closes the same thought as a challenge: publish the offerings, set forth the perfections of the gods you worship, and see what they can do when drought and blasting and famine and pestilence and the sword are sent.
6:
Cleanness of teeth is glossed the same way by all and then made vivid. Clarke reads it as scarcity of bread and turns the irony: they shall have no trouble cleaning their teeth, having nothing to eat. Ellicott identifies it with want of bread by the poetic parallelism and gives the picture behind it, clean sharp teeth projecting from thin lips, one of the ghastly aspects of famine. Keil and Delitzsch note that the adversative opening sets the chastisement against the idolatry just described, the first stroke being famine, as the law had threatened. Wesley puts it as a sequence, that the God who had given many blessings to win them to repentance then tried what judgments might do.

Which famine is meant divides them. Gill rules out the siege famine in Samaria, confined as it was to one city and a short time while this was in all the cities, and prefers the seven-year famine a later prophet foretold. Clarke reports that identification but thinks it likelier the one described by another of the twelve. Neither will settle for the obvious case, and both argue from the scope of the words rather than from any date.

The refrain is where Henry does his work. He counts the five repetitions and reads four things out of them: that what God designed in every rebuke was to bring them back to their allegiance; that had they returned they would have been accepted and the trouble removed; that further trouble came only because the former had not done its work, since it is no pleasure to the Almighty to afflict; and that God took it unkindly to be forced into doing what he did so unwillingly. Clarke hears the same five repetitions as implying God's longsuffering, his various modes of fatherly chastisement, the people's ingratitude and their obstinate wickedness. Ellicott puts it most simply, that the Lord is introduced here grieving over the failure of his own disciplinary treatment.

The withheld rain is dated and then explained. Gill refers it to the three years of drought in an earlier reign, and notes what such a withholding does to man and beast. Clarke fixes the season from an old authority: from the end of April until harvest three months pass without rain there, so what was withheld was the spring rain, particularly April's. Calvin explains why the drought is recorded separately from the famine it caused. Want by itself will be acknowledged as a curse by anyone not wholly stupid; but when drought comes first, and the ground disappoints those who work it, and only then the food fails, men are given more time to think.

The unequal rain is treated as the whole point of the sign. Clarke describes the distinction on the ground: one city filling its cisterns while its neighbour had none, one field watered and abundant while the farm beside it had not a shower. Wesley makes the purpose explicit, that they might see God's hand in it, and sharpens the example until one part of a single field flourished while another lay dry and withered. On the wandering that followed, Gill has the inhabitants of two or three cities going up and down in search of any place with water for themselves and their cattle. Calvin presses how unusual that was, whole cities leaving home to run wherever water was heard of, like wild beasts; and he explains why they were not satisfied, since the fountains could have supplied their own people but were exhausted once such a multitude flowed in from every quarter. Wesley allows a second possibility, that those who had water either had not enough or dared not part with it.
9:
The blights come first, and the glosses are agreed on the mechanism. Gill reads blasting as the scorch carried on an east wind, noting that the Latin version renders it a burning wind, and mildew as the opposite affliction, a clammy dew that settles and rots, named from its yellowness, a kind of jaundice fallen upon the fruits of the earth. Ellicott has the corn burnt up before it is ready to ear, so that the standing crop shows a tawny yellow where it should have ripened toward golden red. What the weather spared the insects finished. Clarke has the blasting and mildew on the field crops and the locusts on gardens and vineyards, and holds that the combination was shown to be a divine judgment rather than an accident of season; Ellicott insists that the creature devours in vast numbers, the Hebrew carrying a plural force the English blunts. Wesley fixes the cruelty of the timing in two words apiece: the increase was destroyed when the trees were at their most fruitful, and the creatures ate up all, as is the manner of them.

Calvin draws out the weight of the sequence. One kind of punishment leaves men guilty enough; but when God tries one way after another and still effects nothing, those who remain stupid under the accumulation are past recovery. That is the argument the refrain carries, and it governs what follows.

The pestilence sent after the manner of Egypt divides them. Gill canvasses three readings without settling: it may be like the plague that took the firstborn; or, following the Targum, in the way of Egypt, which is to say on the wilderness road; or sent upon them as they travelled down into Egypt for help and for food during the famine, an errand that displeased the Lord. Keil and Delitzsch are content to note how closely the pestilence and the sword are set together, the one treading on the heels of the other. Clarke anchors it in the Syrian siege of Samaria, when an ass's head sold for eighty pieces of silver and mothers ate their own children, and the relief came by the unseen slaughter of the besiegers. Ellicott prefers the marginal rendering, with the captivity of your horses, and calls Egypt the birthplace of the plague, citing a scholar who holds that the prophet is explaining the cause of the pestilence itself: hosts of slaughtered warriors left scattered across the camp. Wesley keeps to the plain sense, that the riders were killed and the slaughter so great that too few remained to bury the dead.

The overthrow like Sodom is read narrowly by Gill, of particular houses or persons struck by lightning rather than whole cities burnt. Keil and Delitzsch see the ascent from smaller chastisements to greater, the utter confusion of the state, Israel pulled out only as a brand is pulled from the burning. Clarke insists that both the judgment and the deliverance were evidently from God. Ellicott reads a distinct calamity here, an earthquake and perhaps a volcanic eruption, and appeals to a long series of such shocks distressing that land from the fourth century to the twelfth; he hears in the Sodom allusion a hint of fierce licence in the northern kingdom, prefers among you to some of you, and observes that men would cast such a charred brand back into the fire. Behold then the goodness and the severity of God. Wesley has those who escaped still standing as firebrands in the midst of the fire, spared only because infinite mercy kept a remnant, and Calvin adds that Sodom is what scripture sets before our eyes whenever it paints the wrath of God graphically. Nearly the same ruin fell here, and only a few came out.
12:
What God threatens to do is deliberately not said, and the expositors make that silence the point. Gill notes that nothing is expressly specified, and offers that it must be worse than what had come, or the same things repeated until an utter end was made. Keil and Delitzsch rule out any backward glance: the formula is always used by this prophet to introduce what is about to happen, and the future verb forbids reading it of the chastisements just listed. Their comment on the reticence is the sharpest here: having said, this will I do to thee, He is silent as to what He will do. Ellicott says the same in his own key, that the doom is left in awful uncertainty, wrapt up in the boundless possibilities of divine judgment, and that all which had gone before in famine, drought, blight and earthquake was not final and had failed of its effect. Wesley compresses the whole to a clause: in a more terrible manner will I now proceed against thee. Calvin reads the particle as removing the exception lately allowed, so that extreme punishment now falls without mitigation, since remedies cannot be applied to men past recovery.

Prepare to meet thy God is where they divide. Clarke calls it a military phrase and a challenge to come out to battle: throw yourselves into a posture of defence, summon your idols to your help, and see how far your strength and theirs will avail against the arm of the Lord of hosts. He adds a warning that the verse has been painfully misapplied by public teachers, having no particular relation to the day of judgment nor to the hour of death, and calls such constructions impositions on the text. Gill will not choose between the two senses. Either the words are ironical, feeble worms summoned to muster their forces against the mighty God, who can walk through thorns and briers and burn them up; or they are serious, an exhortation to meet the Lord in the way of his judgments by humiliation, repentance and reformation, not knowing but that he may yet be gracious. Calvin lays out both readings at length and leans to the second, on the ground that the next chapter exhorts to repentance and sets out hope; the prophets, he holds, always moderate the asperity of their doctrine after threatening destruction, since there was at all times some remnant seed, though hidden.

The doxology that closes the chapter is read as a device before it is read as doctrine. Calvin says the accumulation of titles might seem superfluous, but that men whose minds were exceedingly torpid had to be aroused, since when the bare name of God is announced he is neglected by the greatest part of men; something had to be added so that the sleepers might wake and understand how fearful his power is. He notes the two readings of the disputed word, wind or the soul of man, thinks the second more probable because it agrees with the clause that follows, and allows that both may be intended. Ellicott takes it as wind, observes that wind and spirit were closely associated in Hebrew as in Greek under one word, and finds the transition to the next clause natural on that account; he also records that the Greek version rendered the clause as declaring to man his Christ, through a misunderstanding of the original. Gill turns the whole to the person to be met, able to surmount and remove every mountain of difficulty in the way of salvation. Clarke and Wesley end where the verse ends, on the threefold name: the self-existing and independent Being, the God in covenant with mankind, the commander of all the hosts of earth and heaven, whose power all creatures obey and who acts for or against us as he wills.
